newsitem.title: USA: Winds, hail in Illinois, U.S. Midwest seen dry - WSC.
newsitem.headline: Winds, hail in Illinois, U.S. Midwest seen dry - WSC.

text.p: Severe thunderstorms in parts of Illinois Sunday night brought winds up to 75 miles per hour and hail, but crop damage was expected to be limited and U.S. Midwest weather was seen mostly dry this week, a U.S. meteorologist said.
"In general, hail damage and wind damage due to thunderstorms causes very isolated damage," said Joel Burgio, forecaster with Weather Services in Lexington, Mass.
"We're just talking about a few farms, so I would say that the rain did more good than harm," he said.
The severe storms hit the area from Moline, Ill. in the western part of the state and moved south and east toward Peoria in central Illinois, Burgio said.
That system brought only 0.25 to 0.50 inch of rain with heavier amounts in local areas and rainfall coverage for Illinois was put at 25 percent, Burgio said.
Most of the U.S. Midwest is expected to remain dry until the weekend, Burgio said.
"You have to wait for anything that might be more organized until the weekend," Burgio said.

Mostly fair weather was expected Tuesday, but a weak system could bring scattered showers to eastern Minnesota, Wisconsin, northern Illinois and northeastern Iowa. However, minimal coverage is expected, the forecaster said.
Temperatures over the next few days should be cooler, with highs ranging from the 80s to low 90s degrees Fahrenheit on Monday before falling to the 70s and 80s on Tuesday, Burgio said.
At the end of the week, there is the possibility for scattered showers in the western Corn Belt on Saturday into Sunday, and in the eastern Corn Belt on Sunday into Monday, the forecaster said.
